For this article, I'd like to propose a link to a tale written specifically about SCP-627, called The Orb is the Key. This tale provides a lot in the means of a backstory for the object, as well as defines what its original intended purposes was going to be, so I feel as if a simple in-line edit would be sufficient to tie the two together. That being said, proposing the following change:

Editing this:

When not in close (defined as skin contact, or in clothing being worn) contact with a human being, SCP-627 rolls in a circle approximately one meter across.

To read:

When not in close (defined as skin contact, or in clothing being worn) contact with a human being, SCP-627 rolls in a circle approximately one meter across.

If anyone has other/better examples that could be used here please leave a comment saying so!

I downvoted because while I'm not averse to the idea, the execution strikes me as the least interesting way to say "Something anomalous was behind the atomic bomb". It's not good expungement or an engaging story, just some blackboxed letters ans, well, sappy notes that don't convey the gravity of what happened.

If I recall correctly, Albert Einstein actually did very little with the science behind the creation of the bomb. He wrote the initial letter encouraging it, and accounted for the mass difference with the now-annoying (to physicists) E=mc2, but other scientists like Leo Szilard, Oppenheimer, or John von Neumann did the actual work.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
This is pretty bad. The narrative is ham-fisted, clumsy, and obvious, and even if more smoothly executed wouldn't be particularly interesting. It's just SCPifying an element of history, without really saying anything substantive beyond that. Making the source of nuclear weaponry something otherworldly and slightly sinister doesn't add much to your stock "science gone mad" narrative. The notes are sloppy and barely sketched, and while Oppenheimer could certainly be dramatic, that last line forces this directly into B-movie camp. Not to say that's an awful thing, but it's wasted here. As drama it's comically oversketched; as hijinks it's too dour. Downvote.

This was actually supposed to be a reward for him, not a punishment. He got to continue working with it, for the rest of his life, and not have to worry about being killed randomly. At the time this was written, my idea of a d-class was… different. That it wasn't always a bad thing.

Also, this doesn't really come across in the article coherently. The reference to "exemption from monthly termination" makes being a D-Class sound like a decidedly Bad Thing, and in light of the apparently disastrous results of the experiment, if our mysterious Researcher E was indeed assigned to it permanently as a D-Class (which also isn't really coming across) then it comes off very much like punishment. I don't think the article is saying what you think it's saying.
